The inside of the harness: the ReAct loop, how agents find and change code, and how the context window is managed.

slides.title: The ReAct loop, and the loop as code

elements.text: The ReAct loop, and the loop as code
What do I know, what is missing, what is next
Emit a structured call the environment can run
REASON ONLY FAILS: nothing checks the reasoning, and small errors compound into confident hallucination.
ACT ONLY FAILS: tool calls with no plan make the model repeat themselves.
if a final answer is present: return it
The tool message carries role "tool", tool_call_id and content.

slides.title: A coding agent has three components

elements.text: A coding agent has three components
The model reasons and emits actions; the loop runs the model, executes the tools and appends the results.
Tools set capability; guardrails keep it safe. This is where permissions, validation and isolation live.
Context and memory: what the agent knows now, and what it carries forward.
All three share one context window.
THE HARNESS DESIGNER HAS THREE JOBS
1  Assemble the context     2  Validate the request, check permission and run it     3  Optionally process the result and manage context

slides.title: Finding code by name: four approaches

elements.text: Finding code by name: four approaches
In practice: start with grep; reach for an index or LSP when names run out.
Worked example: grep -rn "timeout" src/ returns 37 hits in 12 files; a stack trace points at cart.ts:88 with 3 frames named; textDocument/references returns 42 call sites across 7 files.

Whole-file rewrite: read client.ts, 120 lines into context, write the full file back, 4 lines changed.   Unified diff: @@ -41,3 +41,3 @@, 6 lines and two hunks, applied with git apply patch.diff.   Search and replace: grep -n "retries = 3", then retries = 3 becomes 5.   AST edit: add_param(fetchUser) with a timeout default of 5s, rewriting the signature and all 18 callers, valid by construction.

slides.title: The shell tool: most powerful, most dangerous

elements.text: The shell tool: most powerful, most dangerous
One call can chain, filter, loop and retry.
Filesystem, network, package managers, installed binaries.
Files and processes outlive the call.
Whatever the shell can do, the agent can do.
Its design has to settle five questions:
Isolation answers one question: where the code runs and what it can reach.

Few orthogonal tools: overlapping tools make the model dither
Purpose-built rather than generic: search_orders(customer_id) beats a raw run_sql tool
Token-cheap output: truncate, paginate, summarize. Tool design is context design
Errors that teach: return the fix hint, not just "invalid argument"
Idempotent by default

Browser and visual feedback
Memory and notes: write findings to a file so plans survive compaction
Asking the user
Subagents and delegation
Web search and fetch
One cheap question beats a confident wrong patch.
How should we instruct the model?
"People love coining terms. I use them so you'll know what they mean when you encounter them, but that doesn't mean I agree or like them."
The deck also surveys eight prompting techniques and labels several of them expired. The point: measure techniques, do not memorise them.

slides.title: Context is finite on three axes

elements.text: Context is finite on three axes
Every step re-sends the whole window.
Bigger prompts take longer to prefill and decode.
Recall fades as the window fills, and the middle gets missed, so more context is not better answers.
Both length and position cost accuracy.
ILLUSTRATIVE TOKEN BUDGET FOR ONE AGENT TURN
The slide labels this an illustrative budget, not a measurement.
Context engineering is "the delicate art and science of filling the context window with just the right information for the next step" - Andrej Karpathy.

slides.title: Four stages, from lossless to irreversible

elements.text: Four stages, from lossless to irreversible
Targeted retrieval, tool output shaping, truncation only when shaping cannot, isolation to a subagent.
Progressive tool definition, tool search, tool output offload returning a handle, externalised task list, persistent memory.
Deduplication, observation masking of tool results older than N steps, sliding window.
Rolling summary, or full summary at the limit, reserving headroom, preserving the system prefix, re-injecting critical facts, persisting key facts outside the window via auto memory.
Raw DOM 48,000 tokens becomes prices and headings only, 900 tokens. Same answer.
60 schemas resident 42,000 tokens becomes an index plus 3 schemas, 3,100 tokens. All 60 reachable.
Every result kept, 96,000 tokens, becomes newest state kept, 24,000 tokens. Nothing summarized.
A hallucination enters the window and is later cited as fact.
History grows until the agent imitates its own past actions.
Irrelevant tools and documents steer the answer off course.
New information contradicts old, and both stay unresolved.
The real goal is buried and swapped for a nearby subgoal.
"Name the failure and the fix becomes obvious."   Breunig, "How Contexts Fail and How to Fix Them" (2025)
CHANGING ONLY THE HARNESS DOUBLES ACCURACY
Some apparent "model failures" are actually context- and control-loop failures.

Old tool outputs compacted
Recent observations kept visible
Repetition and stalls detected
Interventions when stuck
Model capability sets the ceiling; the harness determines realized performance.
Source: Lewis, S., "Same Model, Different Harness: Different Coding-Agent Results" (arXiv:2608.26218, 2026)

slides.title: Four things to carry out of Lecture 4

elements.text: Four things to carry out of Lecture 4
An agent is a model plus a loop plus a harness, and the harness sets realized performance.
Context is finite, paid and lossy. Manage it in order: admit, offload, transform, then compact.
Tool design is context design: few orthogonal tools, token-cheap output, errors that teach.
Start with grep; reach for an index or LSP only when names run out.
